-476.d: Forty-fourth year of King Jing of Zhou, with which the Spring and Autumn period ends; the Table of the Six States in the Shiji begins with the next year, the first year of King Yuan of Zhou. Jin is controlled by the four ministerial lineages of Zhi, Zhao, Han and Wei, and Qi is dominated by the Tian lineage, while the Three Huan hold power in Lu and the Seven Mu in Zheng. In the southeast Wu and Yue are locked in a life-and-death struggle, and Yue is about to besiege Wu; Chu has annexed the states north of the Han and in the Yangtze–Huai region, except Sui and Cai, which has moved to Zhoulai. Elsewhere Song, Wey, Zheng and Lu remain, along with Qi, Ju, Zhu, Teng, Xue, Tan, Xu and other states; in the west Qin holds its own against Dali, Yiqu and other Rong; in the north Yan lies off in a corner, and Xianyu (Zhongshan) is established east of the Taihang Mountains.
-476.t: End of the Spring and Autumn

-478.d: Tian Chang of Qi has assassinated Duke Jian (481 BC), and the Tian lineage dominates Qi. Confucius has died (479 BC). After putting down the revolt of Sheng, duke of Bai, King Hui of Chu destroys Chen (478 BC). Goujian, king of Yue, attacks Wu; he and Fuchai draw up their armies on opposite sides of Li Marsh, and he routs the Wu army, after which Wu never recovers.
-478.t: Battle of Li Marsh · Chu destroys Chen

-482.d: Fuchai, king of Wu, opens the He River and goes north to meet the lords at Huangchi, contending with Duke Ding of Jin for leadership of the alliance. Goujian, king of Yue, attacks Wu in its absence, enters the Wu capital and captures Crown Prince You of Wu. Fuchai keeps the news secret, and after swearing the covenant with Jin hurries back south and makes peace with Yue. The next year Tian Chang of Qi assassinates Duke Jian, and in Lu "a qilin is captured on the western hunt", where the text of the Chunqiu ends.

-484.d: Fuchai, king of Wu, cuts the Hangou Canal to link the Yangtze and the Huai (486 BC), and with the army of Lu he attacks Qi and crushes it at Ailing, and the Qi general Guo Shu is captured and killed. Goujian, king of Yue, leads his people to pay court to Wu; Fuchai sends Wu Zixu the sword Shulou, and Zixu cuts his own throat.

-487.d: Duke Jing of Song destroys Cao and seizes Yang, earl of Cao; Song's lands extend to Taoqiu. Fuchai, king of Wu, marches north year after year to attack Chen and Lu, meets Lu at Zeng and demands a hundred sets of sacrificial animals. In Jin the Fan and Zhonghang lineages are gone, and the four ministerial lineages of Zhi, Zhao, Han and Wei share control of the government.

-494.d: Fuchai, king of Wu, defeats Yue at Fujiao and besieges Goujian at Kuaiji; the king of Yue sues for peace with humble words and rich gifts and goes to Wu as a vassal. Wu Zixu remonstrates but is not heeded, and Wu turns north toward the Central Plains. In Jin the Six Ministerial Lineages are at civil war (497–490 BC), and the Fan and Zhonghang lineages are gradually losing; Cai moves to Zhoulai to rely on Wu (493 BC).

-496.d: Helü, king of Wu, attacks Yue during the mourning for Yunchang, king of Yue; Goujian has three ranks of convicts cut their own throats before the battle line, and while the Wu army stares in shock he attacks and routs it at Zuili. Helü, wounded in the foot, dies, and Fuchai succeeds him, vowing to avenge his father. Chu destroys Dun (496 BC) and the next year Hu. Confucius has already left Lu to travel among the states.

-505.d: Shen Baoxu weeps at the Qin court for seven days, and Duke Ai of Qin sends five hundred chariots to rescue Chu, defeating Wu at Ji; Yue takes the chance to invade Wu, and Fugai, the Wu king's younger brother, goes home and makes himself king. The Wu army withdraws, and King Zhao of Chu recovers his state and soon destroys Tang; the next year he moves his capital to Ruo to escape Wu.
-505.t: Qin rescues Chu · King Zhao of Chu recovers his state

-506.d: Cai and Tang, because Zichang, the Chu chief minister, had demanded bribes from them, bring Wu to attack Chu. Helü, king of Wu, Sun Wu and Wu Zixu leave their boats at Huairui, advance from Yuzhang and face Chu across the Han; winning five battles out of five, they crush Chu at Baiju and enter Ying, and Wu Zixu digs up the tomb of King Ping of Chu and flogs his corpse. King Zhao of Chu flees to Sui. The same year Jin meets the lords at Shaoling, and Cai destroys Shen.
-506.t: Battle of Baiju · the Wu army enters Ying

-512.d: Prince Guang of Wu has Zhuan Zhu assassinate King Liao and makes himself king as Helü (515 BC), with Wu Zixu as envoy and Sun Wu as general. Wu has already destroyed Chao and Zhongli (518 BC); in 512 BC it destroys Xu and Zhongwu, and Zhangyu, viscount of Xu, flees to Chu. Wu Zixu "forms three armies to wear Chu down", and Chu is exhausted from rushing to meet each attack. Prince Zhao has fled to Chu (516 BC).

-519.d: King Jing of Zhou has died (520 BC), and Prince Zhao fights the new king, King Jing, for the throne; the Zhou house falls into chaos, with Prince Zhao holding Wangcheng and King Jing living at Diquan. Prince Guang of Wu routs Chu and the armies of Dun, Hu, Shen, Cai, Chen and Xu at Jifu, killing the rulers of Hu and Shen. Jin destroys Gu (520 BC).
-519.t: Battle of Jifu · rebellion of Prince Zhao

-525.d: Xun Wu of Jin, on the pretext of a sacrifice to the Luo, makes a surprise attack and destroys the Luhun Rong; the viscount of Luhun flees to Chu. Wu and Chu fight at Chang'an; Chu captures the Wu king's barge Yuhuang, and Prince Guang of Wu takes it back in a night raid. The viscount of Tan visits the court of Lu, and Confucius goes to learn from him.
-525.t: Jin destroys Luhun · Battle of Chang'an

-529.d: King Ling of Chu attacks Xu and builds the Zhanghua Terrace, and popular resentment boils over; in 529 BC Prince Bi and Qiji rise in revolt, and King Ling hangs himself at Ganxi. Qiji takes the throne as King Ping and restores Chen and Cai (Cai moving to Xincai). Jin destroys Fei of the White Di (530 BC) and meets the lords at Pingqiu, remaining leader of the alliance.
-529.t: Chen and Cai restored · Assembly at Pingqiu

-531.d: King Ling of Chu (on the throne from 541 BC) holds a grand assembly of the lords at Shen (538 BC), attacks Wu, and seizes and kills Qing Feng, a fugitive minister of Qi, at Zhufang. In 534 BC Chu destroys Chen, and in 531 BC it lures Marquis Ling of Cai to his death and destroys Cai, making Qiji duke of Chen and Cai. Zichan of Zheng casts the penal code (536 BC).

-546.d: Xiang Xu of Song launches the second truce to end war: grandees of Jin, Chu, Lu, Wey, Chen, Cai, Zheng, Xu, Cao, Song and other states meet in Song (Qi and Qin also assent) and agree that "the followers of Jin and Chu shall each attend both courts". The two powers share the hegemony, and for more than forty years afterwards the Central Plains see few major wars. Chu destroys Shujiu (548 BC), and all of the Qunshu pass to Chu.

-562.d: Duke Dao of Jin divides his four armies into three to wear Chu down in rotation: "after three campaigns Chu could no longer contend". In 562 BC Zheng finally submits to Jin and after the Assembly at Xiaoyu never rebels again; Jin's hegemony revives. Lu forms three armies, and the Jisun, Shusun and Mengsun divide the ducal house three ways.
-562.t: Assembly at Xiaoyu · Duke Dao regains hegemony

-567.d: Duke Li of Jin is assassinated and Duke Dao comes to the throne (573 BC); Wei Jiang makes peace with the Rong (569 BC), and Jin grows strong again. Duke Ling of Qi destroys Lai and moves Lai to Ni, and Qi holds the whole Jiaodong Peninsula; the same year Ju destroys Zeng. Chu has destroyed Shuyong (574 BC). Zheng still switches back and forth between Jin and Chu.

-575.d: Hua Yuan of Song brokers the first truce to end war (579 BC): Jin and Chu swear a covenant outside the west gate of Song but soon break it. Duke Li of Jin leads the lords against Qin and defeats it at Masui (578 BC). In 575 BC King Gong of Chu comes to the rescue of Zheng and fights Jin at Yanling; the king is hit in the eye, Zifan is too drunk to plan, and the Chu army slips away by night: Jin's hegemony revives.

-584.d: Wuchen, duke of Shen in Chu, flees to Jin with Xia Ji, and Zifan wipes out his clan. Wuchen asks to be sent as envoy to Wu and teaches the people of Wu chariot driving and archery; Wu begins attacking Chu, Chao and Xu and enters Zhoulai, and Zizhong and Zifan of Chu "rush to answer the call seven times in one year". Shoumeng of Wu takes the title of king. Jin moves its capital to Xintian (585 BC).

-589.d: King Zhuang of Chu has died (591 BC). Duke Qing of Qi mocks and insults the Jin envoy Xi Ke; in 589 BC Xi Ke leads the armies of Jin, Lu, Wey and Cao to crush the Qi army at An. Pang Choufu changes places with Duke Qing, who escapes, and Qi returns the fields of Wenyang to Lu. The next year Jin destroys Qianggaoru, the last branch of the Red Di, and forms six armies.

-594.d: Chu besieges Song for nine months (595–594 BC); Hua Yuan of Song slips into the Chu camp at night and makes peace with Chu. Xun Linfu of Jin destroys the Lu lineage of the Red Di, and the next year Shi Hui destroys the Jia lineage and Liuxu; the whole Shangdang region passes to Jin. Duke Xuan of Lu introduces the "first land tax by area", taxing fields by their measured area and so recognising private land.
-594.t: Jin destroys the Red Di · first land tax by area

-597.d: King Zhuang of Chu destroys Shuliao (601 BC) and enters Chen, briefly making it a county (598 BC). In 597 BC Chu besieges Zheng for three months, and the earl of Zheng comes out to meet him bare to the waist, leading a sheep. Xun Linfu of Jin comes to Zheng's rescue and fights Chu at Bi; the Jin army is routed and scrambles for the boats to cross the He: "the fingers in the boats could be scooped up by the handful". King Zhuang of Chu becomes hegemon of the Central Plains.

-606.d: King Zhuang of Chu attacks the Luhun Rong, parades his troops on the outskirts of Zhou, and asks about the size and weight of the Nine Tripods; Wangsun Man replies, "It lies in virtue, not in the tripods." In Jin Zhao Chuan has assassinated Duke Ling (607 BC); Zhao Dun "fled but did not cross the border, and on returning did not punish the assassin", and Dong Hu writes, "Zhao Dun assassinated his lord." Chu's power presses right up to Luoyi.
-606.t: Asking about the tripods of the Central Plains

-611.d: For three years after his accession King Zhuang of Chu has made no sound. When a great famine strikes, the people of Yong lead the Man tribes, and the people of Jun the Hundred Pu, in revolt against Chu; King Zhuang joins forces with Qin and Ba to destroy Yong, and with his first cry astonishes all. Duke Ling of Jin misrules, and Zhao Dun runs the government; Zheng, Song, Chen, Cai and other states waver between Jin and Chu.

-623.d: In 624 BC Duke Mu of Qin attacks Jin, crosses the He and burns his boats, takes Wangguan, and buries the dead at Xiao before returning; after this, on You Yu's advice, he turns to attacking the Western Rong, "adding twelve states and opening up a thousand li of land, and so becoming hegemon of the Western Rong". King Mu of Chu destroys Jiang (623 BC) and the next year Lu and Liao, and Chu's power pushes east to the middle Huai River.
-623.t: Qin becomes hegemon of the Western Rong

-627.d: Wey moves its capital to Diqiu (629 BC). Duke Mu of Qin sends Mengming Shi and others to surprise Zheng; the Zheng merchant Xian Gao feasts the troops, and the Qin army destroys Hua and turns back. Duke Xiang of Jin, in mourning dyed black, joins with the Jiang Rong to wipe out the Qin army in the Xiao Mountains, capturing its three commanders. Jin also defeats the Di at Ji, where Xian Zhen dies in the battle line. The friendship between Qin and Jin is broken.

-632.d: Duke Wen of Jin (on the throne from 636 BC) helps King Xiang of Zhou put down the rebellion of Prince Dai and gains the fields of Yangfan, Wen, Yuan and Cuanmao (Nanyang). Wey destroys Xing (635 BC). In 632 BC Duke Wen, with the armies of Qi and Qin, "withdraws three days' march" and then crushes the Chu army at Chengpu; at the Covenant of Jiantu he is appointed leader of the lords, and Jin's hegemony begins.
-632.t: Battle of Chengpu · Covenant of Jiantu

-638.d: Duke Huan of Qi has died (643 BC), and five princes fight over the succession. Duke Xiang of Song seeks to inherit the hegemony but is seized by Chu at the Assembly at Yu (639 BC); in 638 BC he fights Chu at the Hong and, refusing "to drum against an enemy not yet in formation", is badly defeated and wounded in the thigh. Qin destroys Liang (641 BC) and Rui (640 BC); Qin and Jin move the Luhun Rong to Yichuan. Prince Chong'er of Jin is still wandering in exile among Qi, Cao, Song, Zheng and Chu.
-638.t: Battle of Hong · the Luhun Rong resettled

-645.d: Duke Hui of Jin reneges on the bribe he promised Qin, and when Qin suffers famine he refuses to sell it grain. Duke Mu of Qin attacks Jin, fights at Hanyuan and captures Duke Hui, later releasing him; Jin cedes the land of Hexi and sends Crown Prince Yu as a hostage. Chu has destroyed Huang (648 BC). Guan Zhong dies this year, and Qi's hegemony begins to wane.

-651.d: Duke Huan of Qi meets the lords at Kuiqiu; King Xiang of Zhou sends his steward Kong to present sacrificial meat, and the covenant declares, "All of us who join in this covenant, having sworn it, shall return to good relations": Duke Huan's hegemony reaches its peak. The same year Duke Xian of Jin dies, Li Ke kills Xiqi and Zhuozi, and Duke Mu of Qin installs Yiwu, who becomes Duke Hui of Jin.

-655.d: Duke Xian of Jin again borrows a road through Yu, besieges Shangyang and destroys Guo; on the way back he surprises Yu and seizes the duke of Yu and his grandee Baili Xi: "when the lips are gone, the teeth are cold". Chu destroys Xian. Duke Huan of Qi meets the lords at Shouzhi to secure the position of the royal heir. In Jin, in the Li Ji Unrest, Crown Prince Shensheng has killed himself (656 BC), and Chong'er and Yiwu flee abroad.
-655.t: Borrowing a road to attack Guo

-656.d: Duke Huan of Qi walls Chuqiu and enfeoffs Wey there (658 BC), and Wey lives on. In 656 BC Duke Huan leads the armies of Lu, Song, Chen, Wey, Zheng, Xu and Cao to invade Cai; Cai collapses, and he goes on to attack Chu. Qu Wan comes to swear a covenant at Shaoling, and Guan Zhong rebukes Chu because "the tribute of bundled thatch has not come in". Duke Xian of Jin borrows a road through Yu and takes Xiayang from Guo (658 BC).

-660.d: Duke Xian of Jin forms two armies and destroys Huo, Wei and Geng (661 BC), granting Geng to Zhao Su and Wei to Bi Wan. The Di push south in force, attacking Xing (662 BC) and destroying Wey (660 BC); Duke Yi of Wey dies in battle at Ying Marsh, and the survivors cross the He and set up Duke Dai at Caoyi; Wey's lands north of the He all pass to the Di. Duke Huan of Qi sends Prince Wukui to garrison Caoyi, and also rescues Xing and moves it to Yiyi (659 BC).
-660.t: The Di destroy Wey · Jin destroys Huo, Wei and Geng

-663.d: The Mountain Rong attack Yan; Duke Huan of Qi marches north against the Mountain Rong as far as Guzhu before turning back. Duke Zhuang of Yan escorts him into Qi territory, and Duke Huan cedes to Yan the land as far as the Yan ruler has come. Duke De of Qin has already moved his capital to Yong (677 BC). Duke Xian of Jin (on the throne from 676 BC) wipes out the Huan and Zhuang clans and walls Jiang as his capital. King Cheng of Chu has come to the throne (671 BC), with Ziwen as chief minister running the state.
-663.t: Attack on the Mountain Rong to rescue Yan

-678.d: Duke Wu of Quwo destroys Min, marquis of Jin, at the capital Yi, bribes King Xi of Zhou with the treasure vessels and is appointed marquis of Jin; Jin is reunited. King Wen of Chu destroys Deng, and the whole middle Han River belongs to Chu. Duke Huan of Qi has already met the lords at Juan (679 BC), marking "the beginning of Qi's hegemony", and this year he swears a joint covenant with the lords at You.
-678.t: Quwo supplants Yi · Chu destroys Deng

-680.d: Duke Huan of Qi meets Song, Chen, Cai and Zhu at Beixing (681 BC); the people of Sui stay away, and Qi destroys Sui. He also swears a covenant with Lu at Ke, where Cao Mo seizes him to force terms. Over the affair of Xi Gui, King Wen of Chu destroys Xi and takes Xi Gui. With the two powers Qi and Chu rising in the east and west, the small states of the Central Plains begin to choose which of them to depend on.
-680.t: Chu destroys Xi · Assembly at Beixing

-684.d: After Duke Xiang of Qi is assassinated, Prince Xiaobai and Prince Jiu contend for the throne; Xiaobai gets home first and becomes Duke Huan of Qi, with Guan Zhong as chancellor. Qi attacks Lu; Cao Gui asks to fight, and Lu defeats Qi at Changshao; the same year Qi destroys Tan. In the south King Wen of Chu has already destroyed Shen (c. 688 BC), and he defeats Cai at Shen and captures Marquis Ai of Cai.
-684.t: Battle of Changshao · Qi destroys Tan

-690.d: Duke Xiang of Qi attacks Ji in the name of avenging a wrong done nine generations before; the marquis of Ji "leaves his state for good", and Ji falls to Qi. King Wu of Chu attacks Sui again and dies in the field; Dou Qi, the chief minister, and Qu Chong, the Mo'ao, keep his death secret and force Sui to make peace. King Wen of Chu succeeds him and the next year moves the capital to Ying, setting his sights on Shen and Deng to the north.
-690.t: Qi destroys Ji · death of King Wu of Chu

-704.d: Xiong Tong, ruler of Chu, attacks Sui and asks the people of Sui to seek an honoured title for him from the Zhou king; refused, he makes himself King Wu (704 BC), setting himself up as Zhou's equal. King Wu of Chu destroys Quan and makes it a county, and defeats Sui at Suqi; the states east of the Han tremble. The lords of the Central Plains still regard Chu as the "Jing Man".
-704.t: King Wu of Chu proclaims himself king

-707.d: Duke Zhuang of Zheng grows ever stronger: he enters Xu (712 BC) and repeatedly defeats Song, Wey, Chen and Cai. King Huan of Zhou strips Duke Zhuang of his post as royal minister and leads the armies of Chen, Cai and Wey against Zheng; they fight at Xuge, the royal army is routed, and Zhu Dan shoots the king in the shoulder. The prestige of the Son of Heaven collapses, and the age of the lords contending for hegemony begins. In Jin the Yi and Quwo branches go on attacking each other.

-722.d: First year of Duke Yin of Lu, with which the record of the Chunqiu (Spring and Autumn Annals) begins. Duke Zhuang of Zheng defeats Gongshu Duan at Yan, ending the revolt of his full younger brother, and Zheng is united at home and abroad. Wey, Song, Chen and Cai fall out with Zheng, and the eastern lords attack one another in turn; soon afterwards "Zhou and Zheng exchange hostages" (720 BC): royal authority can no longer command the lords.
-722.t: Spring and Autumn Annals begin · the earl of Zheng defeats Duan

-745.d: Marquis Zhao of Jin enfeoffs his uncle Chengshi at Quwo, with the title Huan Shu. Quwo is larger than the capital Yi, and Shi Fu sighs, "The trunk is already weak; how can it last?" From then on Jin is split into two branches, Yi and Quwo, which contend for sixty-seven years. In the south Fenmao, ruler of Chu, "first opens up the Pu", and Chu begins to expand south of the Yangtze and the Han.

-750.d: Duke Wen of Qin hunts eastward to the Confluence of the Qian and Wei and builds a town there to live in (762 BC); in 750 BC he attacks the Rong, who are defeated and flee, and Qin takes in the remaining Zhou people as its own, its land reaching Mount Qi, while the land east of Mount Qi is presented to Zhou. Qin thus holds the western Guanzhong and becomes the western shield of the Zhou house. In the east the lords each tend their own affairs, with no major campaigns.
-750.t: Qin takes the land west of Mount Qi

-767.d: Duke Wu of Zheng first destroys Kuai (769 BC) and then East Guo (767 BC), and makes the land of Kuai into Xinzheng, founding his state east of the He and the Luo; Zheng thus becomes a strong state in the eastern Central Plains. "When Zhou moved east, it was on Jin and Zheng that it relied": Marquis Wen of Jin and Duke Wu of Zheng are both pillars of the royal house, and Duke Wu of Wey also helps Zhou put down the Rong.

-770.d: In 771 BC the marquis of Shen joins with the Quanrong to storm Haojing and kill King You at the foot of Mount Li; King Ping moves east to Luoyi, and from then on the Zhou house declines. Duke Xiang of Qin, rewarded for escorting the king, is for the first time ranked among the feudal lords, and King Ping promises him the land west of Mount Qi, though the western Guanzhong is still held by the Quanrong. Jin has its capital at Yi; Zheng still keeps its households lodged between Kuai and East Guo. In the east Qi, Lu, Song and Wey, and in the south Chu and Sui, Shen, Xi, Deng and the other states north of the Han each hold their own lands, with the Rong and Di living scattered among them.
-770.t: King Ping moves east · Qin made a feudal state
